bank.title: Muscle Tissue Bank II
bank.source: Junqueira's Basic Histology, 15th ed. · Chapter 10: Muscle Tissue

questions.statement: Contractility is a universal cell property that muscle cells have optimized.
questions.explanation: True. Muscle tissue is defined as cells that optimize the universal property of contractility, using actin microfilaments like all cells.

questions.statement: Muscle is the only tissue whose cells contain actin microfilaments.
questions.explanation: False. Actin microfilaments generate force in ALL cells; muscle only optimizes this universal property.

questions.statement: Muscle contraction drives movement within organ systems, of blood, and of the body as a whole.
questions.explanation: True. The chapter lists all three levels of movement powered by muscle.

questions.statement: Most muscle cells arise from embryonic ectoderm.
questions.explanation: False. Essentially ALL muscle cells are of MESODERMAL origin.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle cells are elongated and often branched.
questions.explanation: True. They are bound to one another at intercalated discs.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are often branched and joined by intercalated discs.
questions.explanation: False. Branched cells joined by intercalated discs describe CARDIAC muscle. Smooth muscle cells are fusiform and unbranched.

questions.statement: Both skeletal and cardiac muscle show cross-striations.
questions.explanation: True. Smooth muscle is the only type lacking striations.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle lacks cross-striations.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle HAS cross-striations; only smooth muscle lacks them.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle is usually, but not always, under voluntary control.
questions.explanation: True. The text says its contraction is quick, forceful and USUALLY under voluntary control.

questions.statement: The word 'sarcolemma' comes from Greek words meaning 'flesh' and 'thing formed'.
questions.explanation: False. Sarcolemma = sarkos (flesh) + lemma (HUSK). 'Thing formed' (plasma) is part of SARCOPLASM.

questions.statement: 'Myo' in myoblast comes from the Latin word for muscle.
questions.explanation: True. L. myo = muscle, so a myoblast is a muscle-forming precursor cell; myoblasts fuse into myotubes.

questions.statement: Muscle specialists give special names to some muscle cell organelles, as neuron specialists do.
questions.explanation: True. Examples are sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum and sarcolemma.

questions.statement: Contraction force comes from changes in the length of actin and myosin filaments.
questions.explanation: False. Force comes from proteins affecting weak actin-myosin crossbridges; the filaments SLIDE without changing length.

questions.statement: Connective tissue layers are found only in skeletal muscle, not in cardiac or smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Thin connective tissue layers surround fibers in ALL THREE types; they are just seen best in skeletal muscle.

questions.statement: The epimysium is made of dense irregular connective tissue.
questions.explanation: True. It is the external sheath around the entire muscle.

questions.statement: The perimysium is the outermost connective tissue sheath of a skeletal muscle.
questions.explanation: False. The EPIMYSIUM is outermost. The perimysium wraps fascicles inside the muscle.

questions.statement: Each fascicle acts as a functional unit whose fibers work together.
questions.explanation: True. Each fascicle is wrapped by perimysium.

questions.statement: The endomysium carries the larger nerves and blood vessels into the muscle.
questions.explanation: False. The larger nerves and vessels travel in septa of EPIMYSIUM; the endomysium holds capillaries and fine nerve fibers.

questions.statement: The endomysium contains reticular fibers and scattered fibroblasts.
questions.explanation: True. It is very thin and delicate.

questions.statement: Lymphatics penetrate the endomysium but never the perimysium.
questions.explanation: False. Nerves, blood vessels and lymphatics PENETRATE THE PERIMYSIUM to supply each fascicle.

questions.statement: Myotendinous junctions show tendon collagen fibers inserting among muscle fibers.
questions.explanation: True. The collagen associates directly with complex sarcolemmal infoldings.

questions.statement: The deep fascia lies beneath the endomysium.
questions.explanation: False. The deep fascia OVERLIES the EPIMYSIUM, outside the whole muscle.

questions.statement: The epimysium is continuous with the tendon at the myotendinous junction.
questions.explanation: True. All three layers and the deep fascia are continuous with the tendon.

questions.statement: Connective tissue in muscle plays no role in transmitting contractile force.
questions.explanation: False. Collagens in these layers TRANSMIT the mechanical force of contracting fibers.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle has endomysium, perimysium and epimysium; smooth muscle has endomysium and less-organized sheaths.
questions.explanation: True. Only skeletal muscle has the full three-layer system; smooth muscle has endomysium plus looser, less-organized sheaths (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Smooth muscle connective tissue is organized into well-defined endomysium, perimysium and epimysium, like skeletal muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle has endomysium plus LESS-ORGANIZED connective tissue sheaths (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: The capillary network of skeletal muscle lies in the endomysium.
questions.explanation: True. It brings O2 to each muscle fiber.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle fibers are single mononucleated cells.
questions.explanation: False. Skeletal fibers are single MULTINUCLEATED cells formed by myoblast fusion.

questions.statement: Myotubes are longer multinucleated tubes formed when myoblasts align and fuse.
questions.explanation: True. Myotubes then make myofilament proteins and begin to show striations.

questions.statement: Satellite cells are fully differentiated muscle fibers that stop contracting.
questions.explanation: False. Satellite cells are UNDIFFERENTIATED reserve myoblasts that never fused.

questions.statement: Satellite cells are mesenchymal cells.
questions.explanation: True. They are a sparse population of mesenchymal cells inside each fiber's external lamina.

questions.statement: Satellite cells are found in large numbers next to each skeletal fiber.
questions.explanation: False. Satellite cells are a SMALL, SPARSE population.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle fibers can be many centimeters long.
questions.explanation: True. Table 10–1 lists cylindrical fibers 10–100 μm wide and many cm long.

questions.statement: Skeletal fibers are fusiform, while cardiac cells are cylindrical.
questions.explanation: False. Both skeletal fibers and cardiac cells are CYLINDRICAL; SMOOTH muscle cells are fusiform (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: The sarcoplasm of skeletal muscle is filled mainly with myofibrils.
questions.explanation: True. Myofibrils run parallel to the fiber's long axis.

questions.statement: Each myofibril is surrounded by its own external lamina.
questions.explanation: False. The external lamina surrounds each muscle FIBER (cell). Myofibrils are inside the fiber, surrounded by SR.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle's key function is voluntary movement (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. Cardiac muscle pumps blood automatically; smooth muscle makes involuntary movements.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle responds to increased load mainly by hyperplasia (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Skeletal muscle responds by HYPERTROPHY (increased fiber size). Only smooth muscle adds hyperplasia.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle fibers show peripheral nuclei, while cardiac and smooth muscle nuclei are central.
questions.explanation: True. Peripheral nuclei under the sarcolemma are unique to skeletal fibers; cardiac and smooth nuclei sit centrally (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: The diaphragm and tongue are made of smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: False. The tongue and diaphragm are SKELETAL muscle (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: The A band is dark in both light microscopy and TEM.
questions.explanation: True. It holds the thick filaments plus overlapping thin filaments.

questions.statement: The I band is named for being anisotropic in polarized light.
questions.explanation: False. I = ISOTROPIC (does not alter polarized light). A = anisotropic.

questions.statement: 'Zwischen', the source of the name Z disc, means 'between'.
questions.explanation: True. The Z disc lies between sarcomeres.

questions.statement: Each myofibril contains thousands of thick and thin filaments in a symmetric pattern.
questions.explanation: True. Their arrangement makes the A and I bands.

questions.statement: Striations are visible only because sarcomeres in neighboring myofibrils are out of register.
questions.explanation: False. Striations show across the fiber because sarcomeres of adjacent myofibrils are in LATERAL REGISTRATION (aligned).

questions.statement: Each sarcomere has one A band and two half I bands.
questions.explanation: True. A sarcomere runs Z to Z, so it includes the central A band and half of the I band on each side.

questions.statement: The I band contains the M line.
questions.explanation: False. The M line is in the middle of the A band, bisecting the H zone. The I band contains the Z disc.

questions.statement: The H zone looks lighter than the rest of the A band because thin filaments do not reach it.
questions.explanation: True. Only myosin tails are there.

questions.statement: The lighter H zone is found at the edge of the A band, next to the I band.
questions.explanation: False. The H zone is at the CENTER of the A band.

questions.statement: 'Mitte', the source of the name M line, means 'middle'.
questions.explanation: True. The M line lies in the middle of the sarcomere.

questions.statement: Myosin and actin make up only a small fraction of striated muscle protein.
questions.explanation: False. Together they are OVER HALF of the total protein.

questions.statement: Hexagonal patterns of filaments in TEM cross sections helped researchers determine filament functions.
questions.explanation: True. These patterns come from the overlap of thin and thick filaments.

questions.statement: Each sarcomere contains only one thick and one thin filament.
questions.explanation: False. Each myofibril has THOUSANDS of each filament type in a symmetric pattern.

questions.statement: Sliding of thin filaments toward the A band center shortens the sarcomere.
questions.explanation: True. The Z discs move toward the ends of the thick filaments.

questions.statement: During contraction, the H zone widens.
questions.explanation: False. The H zone NARROWS as thin filaments slide toward the center; in relaxed muscle it is at its expanded length.

questions.statement: The I band becomes shorter when a skeletal muscle contracts.
questions.explanation: True. In relaxed muscle the I band is at its expanded length.

questions.statement: Thick filaments are 1.0 μm long.
questions.explanation: False. THICK filaments are 1.6 μm long; THIN filaments are 1.0 μm.

questions.statement: Thick filaments are wider than thin filaments (15 nm vs 8 nm).
questions.explanation: True. Thick filaments are 15 nm wide; thin filaments are 8 nm.

questions.statement: Myosin is a small protein of about 50 kDa.
questions.explanation: False. Myosin is a LARGE complex of about 500 kDa.

questions.statement: Myosin heavy chains are described as motor proteins.
questions.explanation: True. They are thin rodlike motor proteins twisted together as tails.

questions.statement: Each myosin molecule has only one globular head.
questions.explanation: False. A globular head forms at one end of EACH of the two heavy chains, so myosin has TWO heads.

questions.statement: Myosin heads have actomyosin ATPase activity.
questions.explanation: True. They bind ATP and catalyze energy release.

questions.statement: Myosin heads bind tropomyosin to form crossbridges.
questions.explanation: False. Myosin heads bind ACTIN to form transient crossbridges. Tropomyosin covers the binding sites.

questions.statement: In a thick filament, the rodlike myosin portions overlap with one another.
questions.explanation: True. Several hundred molecules are arranged with overlapping rods.

questions.statement: Thin filaments are straight, unhelical rods.
questions.explanation: False. Thin actin filaments are HELICAL.

questions.statement: Thin filaments run between the thick filaments.
questions.explanation: True. Overlap makes the dark part of the A band.

questions.statement: The myosin-binding site is on tropomyosin, not on actin.
questions.explanation: False. EACH G-ACTIN monomer has a binding site for myosin.

questions.statement: Tropomyosin is a single polypeptide 400 nm long.
questions.explanation: False. Tropomyosin is a 40-nm coil of TWO polypeptide chains.

questions.statement: TnI is the troponin subunit that regulates the actin-myosin interaction.
questions.explanation: True. TnT attaches to tropomyosin; TnC binds Ca2+.

questions.statement: Troponin has two subunits.
questions.explanation: False. Troponin has THREE subunits: TnT, TnC and TnI.

questions.statement: TnT is the troponin subunit that attaches to tropomyosin.
questions.explanation: True. The 'T' links troponin to Tropomyosin.

questions.statement: α-Actinin anchors thick filaments to the M line.
questions.explanation: False. α-Actinin anchors THIN (actin) filaments at the Z DISC. Myomesin holds thick filaments at the M line.

questions.statement: Actin filaments attach perpendicularly to the Z disc.
questions.explanation: True. They are anchored by α-actinin.

questions.statement: Titin is found mainly in the H zone.
questions.explanation: False. Titin is an important accessory protein of the I BANDS, linking thick filaments to the Z disc.

questions.statement: Titin has both scaffolding and elastic properties.
questions.explanation: True. Its springlike domains span the I band.

questions.statement: Nebulin connects thick filaments to the Z disc.
questions.explanation: False. TITIN connects thick filaments to the Z disc. Nebulin binds THIN filaments.

questions.statement: Nebulin specifies the length of actin polymers during myogenesis.
questions.explanation: True. It binds each thin filament laterally.

questions.statement: Creatine kinase is found in the I band.
questions.explanation: False. Creatine kinase is in the M LINE.

questions.statement: The M line contains a myosin-binding protein and an enzyme that helps regenerate ATP.
questions.explanation: True. Myomesin and creatine kinase.

questions.statement: Phosphocreatine is the enzyme that makes ATP from ADP.
questions.explanation: False. Phosphocreatine is a STORAGE FORM of high-energy phosphate; CREATINE KINASE is the enzyme.

questions.statement: Titin (3700 kDa) is much larger than myosin (~500 kDa).
questions.explanation: True. Titin is the largest protein in the body.

questions.statement: Myosin heavy chains are 1.5 μm long.
questions.explanation: False. Myosin heavy chains are 150 NM long and 2–3 nm thick.

questions.statement: In skeletal muscle, the sarcoplasmic reticulum lies outside the sarcolemma.
questions.explanation: False. The SR is an internal membrane system (smooth ER) that SURROUNDS EACH MYOFIBRIL inside the fiber.

questions.statement: The SR contains pumps and other proteins for sequestering Ca2+.
questions.explanation: True. It stores Ca2+ and releases it on depolarization.

questions.statement: Ca2+ release from the SR is triggered by repolarization of the membrane.
questions.explanation: False. Ca2+ release is triggered by membrane DEPOLARIZATION produced by a motor nerve.

questions.statement: Without T-tubules, Ca2+ release would not occur uniformly throughout a large skeletal fiber.
questions.explanation: True. T-tubules let Ca2+ release happen simultaneously throughout the fiber for uniform contraction of all myofibrils.

questions.statement: T-tubules run parallel to the myofibrils along the length of the fiber.
questions.explanation: False. T-tubules are TRANSVERSE invaginations that penetrate inward and ENCIRCLE each myofibril.

questions.statement: Each T-tubule is part of the sarcolemma.
questions.explanation: True. T-tubules are tubular infoldings of the sarcolemma.

questions.statement: Terminal cisternae are narrow, collapsed regions of the SR.
questions.explanation: False. Terminal cisternae are EXPANDED regions of SR next to each T-tubule.

questions.statement: The triad is best seen in longitudinal TEM sections.
questions.explanation: True. In longitudinal sections the T-tubule and two terminal cisternae appear as a triad.

questions.statement: The central element of a triad is a terminal cisterna.
questions.explanation: False. The central element is the T-TUBULE, flanked by TWO terminal cisternae.

questions.statement: Released Ca2+ enters the cytoplasm around the thick and thin filaments.
questions.explanation: True. This initiates contraction of the sarcomeres.

questions.statement: Cardiac T-tubules form dyads at the Z discs (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. Each dyad has one T-tubule and one terminal cistern.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle T-tubules form dyads like those of cardiac muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle has NO T-tubules; caveolae may be functionally similar (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Caveolae in smooth muscle may be functionally similar to T-tubules (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. They contain ion channels controlling Ca2+ release.

questions.statement: Mitochondria are absent from the region between skeletal myofibrils.
questions.explanation: False. Mitochondria and SR are found BETWEEN the myofibrils.

questions.statement: In a resting muscle, myosin-binding sites on actin are blocked by the troponin-tropomyosin complex.
questions.explanation: True. That is why crossbridges cannot form at rest.

questions.statement: Ca2+ released on stimulation binds myosin heads directly.
questions.explanation: False. Ca2+ binds TROPONIN, which moves tropomyosin to expose actin's binding sites.

questions.statement: Myosin binding to actin produces a conformational change in the myosin head.
questions.explanation: True. This pivot pulls the thin filaments farther into the A band.

questions.statement: The pivot of the myosin head pushes thin filaments out of the A band.
questions.explanation: False. The pivot pulls thin filaments FARTHER INTO the A band.

questions.statement: After the pivot, myosin binds another ATP molecule and detaches from actin.
questions.explanation: True. Then the cycle can repeat.

questions.statement: ATP is not needed for myosin to detach from actin.
questions.explanation: False. Binding ANOTHER ATP is what makes myosin DETACH; without ATP crossbridges stay locked (rigor mortis).

questions.statement: The repeating cycle is attach, pivot, detach and return.
questions.explanation: True. It slides thick and thin filaments past each other.

questions.statement: A single contraction cycle takes about 50 seconds.
questions.explanation: False. Each cycle lasts about 50 MILLISECONDS.

questions.statement: Repeated crossbridge cycles rapidly shorten the sarcomere.
questions.explanation: True. A single contraction results from hundreds of cycles.

questions.statement: When the nerve impulse stops, Ca2+ levels rise further.
questions.explanation: False. When the impulse stops, free Ca2+ DIMINISHES as it is pumped back into the SR.

questions.statement: After the impulse stops, Ca2+ is actively transported back into the SR.
questions.explanation: True. Tropomyosin then re-covers the active sites.

questions.statement: Rigor mortis results from excess Ca2+ pumped into the SR after death.
questions.explanation: False. Rigor mortis results from LACK OF ATP after mitochondria stop, which leaves crossbridges stable.

questions.statement: Rigor mortis develops as mitochondrial activity stops after death.
questions.explanation: True. No ATP means crossbridges cannot detach.

questions.statement: During contraction, the Z discs move apart.
questions.explanation: False. The Z discs are drawn CLOSER together.

questions.statement: During contraction, the Z discs move toward the ends of the thick filaments.
questions.explanation: True. This is how the sarcomere shortens.

questions.statement: Titin is stretched (extended) during contraction.
questions.explanation: False. Titin is COMPRESSED during contraction; it is extended in relaxed muscle.

questions.statement: Titin's springlike action helps the filaments in relaxed muscle.
questions.explanation: True. Titin spans the I band and acts like a spring.

questions.statement: The A band disappears in fully contracted muscle.
questions.explanation: False. The A band stays because thick filaments do not change length; the I band and H zone narrow.

questions.statement: Contraction continues as long as Ca2+ remains bound to troponin.
questions.explanation: True. This keeps the active sites exposed.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle contraction is controlled by the same troponin mechanism as skeletal muscle (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle uses MYOSIN PHOSPHORYLATION by MLCK, triggered by calmodulin binding Ca2+.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle controls contraction in a way similar to skeletal muscle (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. Troponin C binds Ca2+ and moves tropomyosin.

questions.statement: Thick filaments shorten during contraction while thin filaments stay the same.
questions.explanation: False. NEITHER thick NOR thin filaments change length.

questions.statement: Motor nerves enter skeletal muscle myelinated and end as unmyelinated twigs.
questions.explanation: True. The twigs pass through the endomysium to synapse with fibers.

questions.statement: Each motor nerve twig synapses with an entire fascicle at one point.
questions.explanation: False. Each terminal twig forms a synapse with an INDIVIDUAL muscle fiber.

questions.statement: Schwann cells cover the axon branches at their points of contact with muscle cells.
questions.explanation: True. Their external lamina fuses with the sarcolemma's.

questions.statement: Synaptic vesicles at the motor end plate are located in the muscle sarcoplasm.
questions.explanation: False. Synaptic vesicles are in the AXON TERMINAL.

questions.statement: The synaptic cleft lies between the axon terminal and the muscle.
questions.explanation: True. Acetylcholine released from the axon terminal crosses this cleft to reach receptors in the folded sarcolemma.

questions.statement: Junctional folds reduce the number of acetylcholine receptors at the NMJ.
questions.explanation: False. Junctional folds INCREASE surface area and the number of acetylcholine receptors.

questions.statement: Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors in the folded sarcolemma.
questions.explanation: True. This opens cation channels and depolarizes the sarcolemma.

questions.statement: Acetylcholine binding allows Ca2+ to leave the muscle cell, hyperpolarizing it.
questions.explanation: False. Acetylcholine opens a nonselective CATION channel, allowing INFLUX of cations and DEPOLARIZATION.

questions.statement: Acetylcholine quickly dissociates from its receptors.
questions.explanation: True. Free transmitter is then removed by acetylcholinesterase.

questions.statement: Acetylcholinesterase prolongs acetylcholine's contact with its receptors.
questions.explanation: False. Acetylcholinesterase PREVENTS prolonged contact by removing free acetylcholine.

questions.statement: At triads, the depolarization signal triggers Ca2+ release from terminal cisterns.
questions.explanation: True. This starts the contraction cycle.

questions.statement: Motor end plates and neuromuscular junctions are different structures.
questions.explanation: False. They are the SAME synapse; MEP, NMJ and myoneural junction are synonyms.

questions.statement: Extraocular muscles are an example of one motor neuron innervating a single muscle fiber.
questions.explanation: True. This allows precise control of eye movements.

questions.statement: The firing of one motor axon makes tension independent of how many fibers it innervates.
questions.explanation: False. Tension is PROPORTIONAL to the number of fibers the axon innervates.

questions.statement: A muscle with many small motor units allows more precise control.
questions.explanation: True. Number and size of motor units control intensity and precision.

questions.statement: All fibers in a muscle fascicle contract at the same time.
questions.explanation: False. To vary force, fibers within a fascicle do NOT all contract at the same time.

questions.statement: Individual striated muscle fibers contract either all the way or not at all.
questions.explanation: True. They do not show graded contraction.

questions.statement: Cardiac and smooth muscle have motor (somatic) efferent innervation (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac and smooth muscle have AUTONOMIC innervation; skeletal muscle has MOTOR.

questions.statement: Proprioceptors send information from the CNS to the muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Proprioceptors are SENSORY: they send data FROM the musculoskeletal system TO the CNS.

questions.statement: Muscle spindles lie among the muscle fascicles.
questions.explanation: True. They act as stretch detectors.

questions.statement: Muscle spindles contain no muscle fibers, only nerve endings.
questions.explanation: False. Spindles contain a few thin INTRAFUSAL muscle fibers plus sensory axons.

questions.statement: The spindle capsule has concentric layers of flattened cells and contains interstitial fluid.
questions.explanation: True. It is modified perimysium.

questions.statement: Ordinary muscle fibers surrounding the spindle are called intrafusal fibers.
questions.explanation: False. Surrounding ordinary fibers are EXTRAFUSAL. Fibers inside the spindle are intrafusal.

questions.statement: Body movements that stretch extrafusal fibers are detected by muscle spindles.
questions.explanation: True. Sensory nerves relay this to the spinal cord.

questions.statement: Muscle spindle information is relayed only to the cerebral cortex, not the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: False. Spindle sensory nerves relay information to the SPINAL CORD.

questions.statement: Spindle reflexes help regulate the activity of opposing muscle groups during walking.
questions.explanation: True. They also help maintain posture.

questions.statement: Golgi tendon organs enclose sensory axons that penetrate among collagen bundles.
questions.explanation: True. They are at the myotendinous junction.

questions.statement: Golgi tendon organs are unencapsulated free nerve endings.
questions.explanation: False. Golgi tendon organs are ENCAPSULATED structures.

questions.statement: Tendon organs act to inhibit motor nerve activity when tension is excessive.
questions.explanation: True. They protect against excessive force.

questions.statement: Muscle spindles and tendon organs both detect decreases in tension.
questions.explanation: False. Both proprioceptors detect INCREASES in tension.

questions.statement: Proprioceptors help regulate the effort needed for movements that need variable force.
questions.explanation: True. Both spindles and tendon organs contribute.

questions.statement: All skeletal muscle fibers have the same metabolic properties.
questions.explanation: False. Fibers vary in contraction speed and ATP pathway, falling into three major types.

questions.statement: Fiber diversity comes partly from varied expression of contractile or regulatory protein isoforms.
questions.explanation: True. Factors affecting O2 delivery and use also differ.

questions.statement: Histochemical staining cannot distinguish fast from slow fibers.
questions.explanation: False. Histochemical staining identifies fibers with different amounts of 'fast' and 'slow' ATPases.

questions.statement: Capillary density, mitochondrial number, glycogen and myoglobin levels reflect metabolic differences between fibers.
questions.explanation: True. These are histological features of fiber types.

questions.statement: Myoglobin is similar to collagen in structure.
questions.explanation: False. Myoglobin is a globular protein similar to HEMOGLOBIN.

questions.statement: Fresh tissue rich in slow oxidative fibers looks dark or red.
questions.explanation: True. Because of many mitochondria, capillaries and much myoglobin.

questions.statement: Slow oxidative fibers are adapted for short bursts and fatigue quickly.
questions.explanation: False. Slow oxidative fibers contract slowly over LONG periods WITHOUT fatigue.

questions.statement: Fast glycolytic fibers appear white.
questions.explanation: True. They have few mitochondria or capillaries and little myoglobin.

questions.statement: Fast glycolytic fibers have many capillaries.
questions.explanation: False. Fast glycolytic fibers have FEW mitochondria and FEW capillaries.

questions.statement: Lactic acid buildup causes rapid fatigue in fast glycolytic fibers.
questions.explanation: True. It comes from glycolysis during rapid contractions.

questions.statement: Fast oxidative-glycolytic fibers fatigue faster than fast glycolytic fibers.
questions.explanation: False. FOG fibers are INTERMEDIATE; fast glycolytic fibers fatigue FASTEST.

questions.statement: A fiber's metabolic type depends on its motor nerve supply.
questions.explanation: True. It is set by the rate of impulse conduction along the motor nerve.

questions.statement: Most skeletal muscles contain only one fiber type.
questions.explanation: False. Most muscles contain a MIXTURE of fiber types.

questions.statement: Needle biopsies to identify fiber types help diagnose myopathies and motor neuron diseases.
questions.explanation: True. They also help find other causes of muscle atrophy.

questions.statement: Fiber types exist only in skeletal muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Different fiber types also exist in CARDIAC muscle and SMOOTH muscle.

questions.statement: Type IIb fibers have large motor units (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. Type I small; IIa intermediate.

questions.statement: Type I fibers have large motor units (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Type I fibers have SMALL motor units and small diameter.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers have intermediate glycogen content (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. Glycogen content rises from type I (low) to IIa (intermediate) to IIb (high), matching reliance on glycolysis (Table 10–2).

questions.statement: Type IIb fibers have high myoglobin and are red (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Type IIb have LOW myoglobin and are WHITE fibers.

questions.statement: Type IIb fibers have high glycolytic enzyme activity (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. They depend on anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers have sparse mitochondria (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Type IIa fibers have NUMEROUS mitochondria and capillaries.

questions.statement: Type I fibers have low myosin-ATPase activity and slow contraction (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. Types IIa and IIb are high and fast.

questions.statement: Type IIb fibers rely mainly on oxidative phosphorylation (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Type IIb rely on ANAEROBIC GLYCOLYSIS.

questions.statement: Extraocular muscles are a typical location of type IIb fibers (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. They need rapid contraction.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers fatigue more slowly than type I fibers (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Fatigue rate: type I SLOW, IIa INTERMEDIATE, IIb FAST.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers have intermediate fiber diameter (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: True. Type I small; IIb large.

questions.statement: Developing cardiac muscle cells form complex junctions between interdigitating processes instead of fusing.
questions.explanation: True. This differs from skeletal muscle, where myoblasts fuse.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle develops from mesenchyme around the primitive gut tube.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle develops from mesenchymal cells around the primitive HEART TUBE.

questions.statement: The heart is made of tightly knit bundles of cells interwoven in spiraling layers.
questions.explanation: True. This gives a wringing wave of contraction.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle cells are 10–100 μm in diameter and many centimeters long.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac cells are 15–30 μm wide and 85–120 μm long. The first description fits skeletal fibers.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle has a striated banding pattern comparable to skeletal muscle.
questions.explanation: True. Its sarcomeres are organized similarly.

questions.statement: Most cardiac muscle cells have many nuclei, like skeletal fibers.
questions.explanation: False. Each cardiac cell usually has ONE nucleus (sometimes two), centrally located.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle cells may have one or two central nuclei.
questions.explanation: True. Cardiac cells usually have one central nucleus, sometimes two; unlike multinucleated skeletal fibers.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle has no perimysium.
questions.explanation: False. A THICKER perimysium separates bundles and layers of cardiac muscle fibers.

questions.statement: The 'cardiac skeleton' is made of fibrous connective tissue.
questions.explanation: True. It forms from perimysium in specific areas.

questions.statement: Intercalated discs are the same as the cross-striations of cardiac muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Intercalated discs are IRREGULAR, widely spaced junctions between cells; striations are much more closely spaced and regular.

questions.statement: Intercalated discs are steplike and irregular.
questions.explanation: True. They have transverse and longitudinal regions.

questions.statement: Longitudinal regions of intercalated discs are more abundant than transverse regions.
questions.explanation: False. Longitudinal regions are LESS ABUNDANT than transverse regions.

questions.statement: Fascia adherens junctions are found in the transverse regions of intercalated discs.
questions.explanation: True. Together with desmosomes they give strong adhesion.

questions.statement: Gap junctions in intercalated discs run perpendicular to the myofibrils.
questions.explanation: False. Gap junctions are in the LONGITUDINAL regions, running PARALLEL to the myofibrils.

questions.statement: Gap junctions in intercalated discs promote rapid impulse conduction through many cardiac cells.
questions.explanation: True. They let many adjacent cells contract as a unit.

questions.statement: Desmosomes act as 'electrical synapses' in cardiac muscle.
questions.explanation: False. GAP JUNCTIONS act as electrical synapses. Desmosomes give adhesion.

questions.statement: Cardiac mitochondria occupy a larger share of cell volume than those of slow oxidative skeletal fibers.
questions.explanation: True. They occupy up to 40% of cardiac cell volume.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle stores its main fuel as triglycerides in small lipid droplets.
questions.explanation: True. Fatty acids are the heart's major fuel.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle cells contain no glycogen.
questions.explanation: False. Glycogen granules MAY be present, along with lipid droplets and lipofuscin.

questions.statement: In atrial muscle, T-tubules are much smaller or absent.
questions.explanation: True. Ventricular T-tubules are well developed.

questions.statement: Cardiac SR is better organized than skeletal SR.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac SR is LESS well-organized than skeletal SR.

questions.statement: A cardiac dyad has one T-tubule and one terminal cistern.
questions.explanation: True. Junctions involve only one structure of each type.

questions.statement: Cardiac T-tubules lie at the A–I junctions.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac (ventricular) T-tubules lie near the Z DISCS.

questions.statement: Cultured cardiac muscle cells keep contracting, showing that contraction is intrinsic.
questions.explanation: True. Cardiac contraction is intrinsic and spontaneous.

questions.statement: The heartbeat is initiated by motor neurons from the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: False. Impulses are initiated locally by NODES of specialized myocardial fibers; autonomic nerves only adjust the rate.

questions.statement: Autonomic nerves modify the heart rate at the nodes of conducting cells.
questions.explanation: True. Sympathetic speeds it up; parasympathetic slows it.

questions.statement: Individual cardiac fibers show graded contraction.
questions.explanation: False. Contraction of individual myocardial fibers is ALL-OR-NONE.

questions.statement: Atrial granules are associated with small Golgi complexes near the nucleus.
questions.explanation: True. They are 0.2–0.3 μm and contain ANF.

questions.statement: ANF acts mainly on target cells in the liver.
questions.explanation: False. ANF acts on target cells in the KIDNEY to affect Na+ excretion and water balance.

questions.statement: Atrial contractile cells also serve an endocrine function.
questions.explanation: True. They secrete atrial natriuretic factor.

questions.statement: The key function of cardiac muscle is voluntary movement (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle's key function is AUTOMATIC (involuntary) pumping of blood.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle's capacity for regeneration is very poor (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. It lacks satellite cells.

questions.statement: Table 10–1 lists cardiac cells as cylindrical, 10–20 μm in diameter and 50–100 μm long.
questions.explanation: True. Table 10–1 gives these values. The text gives 15–30 μm × 85–120 μm for MATURE cells; either way they are far smaller than skeletal fibers.

questions.statement: Intercalated discs have many adherent and gap junctions (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. These are special structural features of cardiac muscle.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle is found in the walls of large arteries.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle is found in the HEART. Blood vessels have SMOOTH muscle (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Muscle of the heart ventricles is thicker than that of the atria because it pumps blood through the circulation.
questions.explanation: True. Ventricles do the main pumping.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle is specialized for fast, powerful contraction.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle is specialized for SLOW, STEADY contraction.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle contraction is influenced by autonomic nerves and various hormones.
questions.explanation: True. It is not under voluntary control.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle is a minor component of blood vessels.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle is a MAJOR component of blood vessels and of the digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive tracts.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are elongated, tapering and unstriated.
questions.explanation: True. They are also called visceral muscle.

questions.statement: The endomysium of smooth muscle is made mainly of type II collagen.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle endomysium is TYPE I and TYPE III collagen fibers.

questions.statement: The shortest smooth muscle cells are found in small blood vessels.
questions.explanation: True. Smooth muscle cells range from about 20 μm in small blood vessels to 500 μm in the pregnant uterus.

questions.statement: The nucleus of a smooth muscle cell lies at one tapered end.
questions.explanation: False. The single nucleus lies at the CENTRAL, BROADEST part of the cell.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells stain uniformly along their length.
questions.explanation: True. They have no striations.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle cells are linked by numerous GAP JUNCTIONS; intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle.

questions.statement: A contracted smooth muscle cell has a distorted nucleus.
questions.explanation: True. Its borders also become scalloped.

questions.statement: Mitochondria and Golgi of smooth muscle are concentrated at the tapered ends of the cell.
questions.explanation: False. Mitochondria, polyribosomes, RER and Golgi are concentrated NEAR THE NUCLEUS.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells have numerous small plasmalemma invaginations resembling caveolae.
questions.explanation: True. They compartmentalize signaling components.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells have no sarcoplasmic reticulum at all.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle has RUDIMENTARY sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.statement: T-tubules are unnecessary in smooth muscle because its cells are small, tapering and joined by many gap junctions.
questions.explanation: True. That is the textbook's explanation.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle filaments are arranged in myofibrils with sarcomeres.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle filaments CRISSCROSS obliquely and do NOT form sarcomeres.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle uses calmodulin and Ca2+-sensitive MLCK to produce contraction.
questions.explanation: True. Its actin lacks troponin and tropomyosin.

questions.statement: Calmodulin is the enzyme that phosphorylates myosin in smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Calmodulin is the Ca2+-BINDING protein. MLCK (myosin light-chain kinase) phosphorylates myosin.

questions.statement: Dense bodies are functionally similar to Z discs.
questions.explanation: True. Actin filaments insert into them.

questions.statement: Dense bodies are found only deep in the cytoplasm, never at the cell membrane.
questions.explanation: False. Dense bodies are found BOTH in the cytoplasm AND associated with the plasmalemma.

questions.statement: Desmin intermediate filaments attach to dense bodies.
questions.explanation: True. They form an elaborate 10-nm array.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle intermediate filaments are about 25 nm wide.
questions.explanation: False. They are 10-nm intermediate filaments of desmin.

questions.statement: Dense bodies transmit contractile force both within cells and between adjacent cells.
questions.explanation: True. Submembranous dense bodies include desmosomal cadherins.

questions.statement: Peristalsis depends only on the contraction of individual smooth muscle cells, not connective tissue.
questions.explanation: False. The endomysium and other connective tissue layers help COMBINE smooth muscle forces into concerted actions like peristalsis.

questions.statement: In smooth muscle, contraction causes each cell to shorten individually.
questions.explanation: True. Thin filaments pull on dense bodies throughout the cell, so each cell shortens on its own, and its nucleus becomes distorted.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle is under voluntary motor control.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle is NOT under voluntary control.

questions.statement: Contraction of smooth muscle is most commonly stimulated by autonomic nerves.
questions.explanation: True. Hormones and paracrine signals also act.

questions.statement: Oxytocin from the pituitary controls smooth muscle of the bladder.
questions.explanation: False. The textbook names oxytocin as controlling smooth muscle of the UTERUS.

questions.statement: Autonomic varicosities lie in close contact with smooth muscle fibers.
questions.explanation: True. They are periodic swellings of autonomic axons.

questions.statement: A transmitter released from a varicosity acts on only one smooth muscle cell.
questions.explanation: False. The transmitter diffuses and binds receptors on NUMEROUS muscle cells.

questions.statement: Gap junctions let smooth muscle cells contract synchronously or in a coordinated way.
questions.explanation: True. Stimulation spreads to more distant fibers through them.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are less active than fibroblasts in making ECM, contributing nothing to it.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle cells SUPPLEMENT fibroblast activity, making collagen, elastin and proteoglycans.

questions.statement: Active ECM synthesis by smooth muscle may reflect less specialization for strong contraction.
questions.explanation: True. This compares with skeletal and cardiac muscle.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are 0.2–10 mm in diameter (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. The units are MICROMETERS: 0.2–10 μm in diameter, 50–200 μm long.

questions.statement: In smooth muscle, actin-myosin binding requires myosin phosphorylation (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. MLCK does this when calmodulin binds Ca2+.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle special structural features include triads and intercalated discs (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle features are GAP JUNCTIONS, CAVEOLAE and DENSE BODIES.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle is found in the uterus and bladder (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. Also blood vessels and digestive and respiratory tracts.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle contractions are always triggered by nerves and are never spontaneous (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle contractions are partial, slow, and OFTEN SPONTANEOUS, wavelike and rhythmic.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle's capacity for regeneration is good, through mitosis of its cells (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: True. Unlike skeletal (limited) and cardiac (very poor).

questions.statement: The three adult muscle types have the same regenerative potential.
questions.explanation: False. They differ: skeletal limited, cardiac very poor, smooth good (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Even though skeletal muscle cells cannot divide, the tissue shows limited regeneration.
questions.explanation: True. Satellite cells provide new fibers.

questions.statement: Satellite cells are normally highly active and dividing in uninjured muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Satellite cells are normally QUIESCENT until activated by injury.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle shows good regenerative capacity throughout adult life.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle shows very little regeneration beyond EARLY CHILDHOOD.

questions.statement: Myocardial infarcts are generally repaired by connective tissue, forming scars.
questions.explanation: True. Proliferating fibroblasts form myocardial scars.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle regenerates slowly because its cells are large and highly differentiated.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle regenerates RAPIDLY because its cells are SMALL and relatively LESS differentiated.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells are mononucleated.
questions.explanation: True. Simpler, smaller mononucleated cells allow a more active regenerative response.

questions.statement: Fibroblasts are the main source of new smooth muscle cells after injury.
questions.explanation: False. Viable SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS undergo mitosis to replace damaged tissue; pericytes help in vessels.

questions.statement: Pericytes are contractile cells in the walls of small blood vessels.
questions.explanation: True. They help repair vascular smooth muscle.

questions.statement: From outside in, the order is muscle → fascicle → muscle fiber → myofibril → myofilament.
questions.explanation: True. Epimysium wraps the muscle, perimysium each fascicle, endomysium each fiber; fibers contain myofibrils built of thick and thin myofilaments.

questions.statement: Myofibrils are 1–2 μm wide, while whole skeletal fibers are 10–100 μm wide.
questions.explanation: True. So each fiber holds many myofibrils side by side.

questions.statement: The sequence of skeletal muscle excitation is NMJ → sarcolemma → T-tubules → terminal cisternae → Ca2+ release.
questions.explanation: True. The action potential travels along the sarcolemma and T-tubules to the triads, where SR releases Ca2+.

questions.statement: Both Ca2+ and ATP must be present for crossbridge cycling to continue.
questions.explanation: True. In their continued presence the attach-pivot-detach events repeat.

questions.statement: Motor axons branch more in large muscles with coarse movements than in muscles needing precise control.
questions.explanation: True. Coarse muscles have axons innervating 100+ fibers; precise ones like extraocular muscles approach one fiber per neuron.

questions.statement: At the NMJ, the axon terminal sits in a trough on the muscle fiber surface.
questions.explanation: True. The dilated termination of each axonal branch lies in a trough of the sarcolemma.

questions.statement: The H zone contains the M line.
questions.explanation: True. The M line bisects the H zone at the center of the A band.

questions.statement: The I band contains thin filaments, the Z disc and parts of titin.
questions.explanation: True. Titin is an important accessory protein in I bands, connecting thick filaments to the Z disc.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers resemble type I in oxidative metabolism but type IIb in contraction speed.
questions.explanation: True. Type IIa: oxidative phosphorylation (like type I) and fast contraction with high myosin-ATPase (like IIb) (Table 10–2).

questions.statement: Fiber diameter increases from type I to type IIa to type IIb.
questions.explanation: True. Small, intermediate, large (Table 10–2).

questions.statement: Cardiac and smooth muscle both have centrally located nuclei.
questions.explanation: True. Only skeletal muscle has peripheral nuclei (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Both cardiac muscle and smooth muscle spread excitation from cell to cell through gap junctions.
questions.explanation: True. Cardiac gap junctions are in the intercalated discs; smooth muscle cells are linked by numerous gap junctions.

questions.statement: Skeletal and cardiac fibers both contract in an all-or-none manner.
questions.explanation: True. Skeletal is triggered at motor end plates; cardiac is intrinsic, beginning at conducting nodes (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells have fewer, less regularly arranged crossbridges than striated muscle.
questions.explanation: True. Myosin filaments are less regular among the thin filaments, with fewer crossbridges.

questions.statement: α-Actinin is found in both Z discs of striated muscle and dense bodies of smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: True. In both it anchors thin actin filaments.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle has the best-developed SR of the three muscle types.
questions.explanation: True. Skeletal SR is well-developed; cardiac is less; smooth is irregular and rudimentary (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Smooth muscle cells in the pregnant uterus can be about 25 times longer than those in small blood vessels.
questions.explanation: True. They range from 20 μm in small vessels to 500 μm in the pregnant uterus (500 ÷ 20 = 25).

questions.statement: Skeletal fibers are innervated at motor end plates, while cardiac contraction starts at nodes of conducting fibers.
questions.explanation: True. Table 10–1 contrasts these triggers of contraction.

questions.statement: Of the three muscle types, only smooth muscle lacks both striations and T-tubules.
questions.explanation: True. Skeletal and cardiac are striated with T-tubules; smooth muscle has neither (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Myofibrils are wider than whole muscle fibers.
questions.explanation: False. Myofibrils (1–2 μm) are INSIDE fibers (10–100 μm); each fiber has many myofibrils.

questions.statement: From outside in: myofibril → muscle fiber → fascicle → muscle.
questions.explanation: False. That is INSIDE OUT. From outside in: muscle → fascicle → fiber → myofibril → myofilament.

questions.statement: Ca2+ is released from the SR before the action potential reaches the T-tubules.
questions.explanation: False. The action potential travels along T-tubules FIRST; depolarization at triads then triggers Ca2+ release.

questions.statement: Only ATP, not Ca2+, is needed for crossbridge cycling to continue.
questions.explanation: False. BOTH Ca2+ and ATP are needed; without Ca2+ tropomyosin re-covers the binding sites.

questions.statement: At the NMJ, the axon terminal sits on a ridge projecting from the muscle surface.
questions.explanation: False. Each axon terminal lies in a TROUGH on the muscle cell surface.

questions.statement: Precise muscles have motor axons that each innervate more fibers than coarse muscles do.
questions.explanation: False. Precise muscles have FEW fibers per axon (even one); coarse muscles have 100 or more.

questions.statement: The Z disc lies within the H zone.
questions.explanation: False. The Z disc bisects the I BAND. The M line lies within the H zone.

questions.statement: The H zone contains thin filaments but no thick filaments.
questions.explanation: False. The H zone has the rodlike parts of THICK filaments and NO thin filaments.

questions.statement: Type IIa fibers resemble type IIb in metabolism, depending on anaerobic glycolysis.
questions.explanation: False. Type IIa use OXIDATIVE phosphorylation like type I. Only IIb rely on anaerobic glycolysis (Table 10–2).

questions.statement: Fiber diameter decreases from type I to type IIa to type IIb.
questions.explanation: False. It INCREASES: type I small, IIa intermediate, IIb large (Table 10–2).

questions.statement: Cardiac and skeletal muscle both have peripheral nuclei.
questions.explanation: False. Only SKELETAL muscle has peripheral nuclei. Cardiac nuclei are CENTRAL (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle cells are not connected by gap junctions.
questions.explanation: False. Gap junctions fill the longitudinal regions of intercalated discs, coupling cells electrically.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle contractions are all-or-none, like skeletal and cardiac (Table 10–1).
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle contractions are PARTIAL and slow; skeletal and cardiac are all-or-none.

questions.statement: Smooth muscle has more crossbridges than striated muscle because its filaments crisscross.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle has FEWER crossbridges and a less regular myosin arrangement.

questions.statement: α-Actinin is found in skeletal Z discs but not in smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: False. Smooth muscle DENSE BODIES contain α-actinin too.

questions.statement: Cardiac muscle has the best-developed SR of the three muscle types.
questions.explanation: False. SKELETAL muscle has the best-developed SR; cardiac SR is less well-organized (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Satellite cells are found inside the external lamina of cardiac muscle cells.
questions.explanation: False. Cardiac muscle LACKS satellite cells.

questions.statement: Skeletal muscle contraction starts spontaneously at pacemaker nodes.
questions.explanation: False. Skeletal contraction is triggered at MOTOR END PLATES. Pacemaker nodes start CARDIAC contraction.

questions.statement: Of the three muscle types, only cardiac muscle lacks T-tubules.
questions.explanation: False. SMOOTH muscle lacks T-tubules. Cardiac muscle has T-tubules (forming dyads) (Table 10–1).

questions.statement: Peripheral nuclei are found in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle alike.
questions.explanation: False. Peripheral nuclei are UNIQUE to skeletal muscle fibers.

questions.statement: Type I fibers have high glycolytic enzyme activity and low capillary density (Table 10–2).
questions.explanation: False. Type I have LOW glycolytic activity and NUMEROUS capillaries.

questions.statement: Golgi tendon organs are found among muscle fascicles, and muscle spindles in tendons.
questions.explanation: False. Reversed: MUSCLE SPINDLES are among fascicles; GOLGI TENDON ORGANS are at the myotendinous junction.

questions.statement: Myotendinous junctions connect the endomysium directly to the periosteum without involving the epimysium or perimysium.
questions.explanation: False. ALL THREE layers plus the deep fascia are continuous with the tendon at myotendinous junctions.
